COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the penal law, in relation to the definition of rate evasion
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S4900

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the penal law, in relation to the definition of rate
evasion

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

More and more reports are occurring of New York residents, especially
those living in New York City, registering their vehicles out of the
state and also applying for auto insurance policies claiming the vehicle
will be principally garaged and driven in the other state when they
actually use the vehicle primarily in New York State. As a result, the
State and local governments are missing out on millions of dollars in
revenue for registration fees, license plate fees, title fees and a
vehicle use tax in the case of New York City residents. In addition, it
corrupts auto insurance rates because claims are not properly assigned
to the correct rating territory.  This bill would impose a penalty for
the crime of intentional rate evasion, thereby deterring New Yorkers who
may consider committing rate evasion from doing so and in the process
saving law-abiding New Yorkers from the costs incurred by rate evasion.

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Amends the Penal Law under the article for insurance fraud by
adding a new section 176.75 for the crime of rate evasion. Defines rate
evasion as insuring a vehicle in a state other than New York when the
vehicle is principally used and garaged in New York Provides exceptions
for persons who insure a motor vehicle in another state where they have
a second residence and for college students.

Section 2. The bill would take effect on the first day of November next
succeeding the date on which it becomes a law.

JUSTIFICATION:

The New York State Commission of Investigation (SCI) in 2006 published a
preliminary report of their investigation into insurance rate evasion
through the use of out of New York State license plates. SCI found that
in 2005 295,963 parking summonses were issued in New York City to
127,243 Pennsylvania registered vehicles. As of February 2006, 152,957
of these summonses were still outstanding and these represent unpaid
fines due to New York City of $14.3 million.  New York City is also
missing out on unpaid red light traffic infraction fines due to out of
state registrations. In 2005 7,378 notices were sent to owners of vehi-
cles registered in Pennsylvania with 3,143 remaining unpaid as of March
2006. The unpaid fines for these notices add up to $270,350.

Additional evidence of the large number of New Yorkers improperly regis-
tering their vehicles out of state is found from the SCI report's reci-
tation of 2004 data with 4,495 accidents involving Pennsylvania-regis-

tered vehicles reported to DMV with 1,098 of these accidents (about a
quarter) occurring in Brooklyn. Since Brooklyn is not contiguous with
Pennsylvania, this strongly suggests that most of the owners of these
vehicles were likely New York residents and not Pennsylvania residents.

Furthermore, the New York Department of Financial Services' Financial
Frauds & Consumer Protection Unit (FFCPU) 2012 Annual Report showed that
the total amount of reported premium lost in 2012 due to rate evasion by
New Yorkers improperly insuring their vehicles out of state was over $3
million. In total numbers, the FFCPU determined that in 2012 3,961
improperly insured vehicles were for out of state insured vehicles.

This measure is modeled on New Jersey's recent rate evasion legislation,
which passed both houses of their legislature unanimously and is await-
ing the Governor's approval. New York should join its nearby sister
state and crack down on this unlawful practice that costs law-abiding
New York auto insurance consumers.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is a new bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

For New York City, recovery of $17.2 million. The State could recoup at
least $3.8 million.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect on the first day of November next succeeding
the date on which it shall have become a law.
